plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a color-coded periodic table of the elements annotated with the most common ionic charges formed by main-group and selected transition-metal elements, illustrating the relationship between an element's position in the table and its tendency to form ions. Group 1 elements (Li+, Na+, K+, Rb+, Cs+, Fr+, shaded purple) and Group 2 elements (Be2+, Mg2+, Ca2+, Sr2+, Ba2+, Ra2+, shaded green) form cations with charges equal to their group number, while nonmetals in Groups 15–17 (shaded pink) form anions such as N3−, O2−, F−, P3−, S2−, Cl−, and their congeners, with negative charges reflecting how many groups they lie to the left of the noble gases. Transition metals in the central d-block (shaded tan) display variable charges — for example Cr3+/Cr6+, Fe2+/Fe3+, Cu+/Cu2+, and Au+/Au3+ — demonstrating that their ionic behavior is not reliably predicted by group position alone. Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn, shaded blue) carry no charge label, reflecting their chemical inertness. This figure establishes the periodic trends in ion formation and marks the boundary where the group-number rule reliably predicts ionic charge versus where transition-metal variability and other exceptions require additional consideration.

interactionPlan.concept: An element’s position in the periodic table often predicts its most common ionic charge, but transition metals and some heavier elements show important variability that the simple group-number rule cannot predict.

interactions.teaches: A single element’s common ion charge can be connected to its valence electron configuration and to the rule, exception, or transition-metal variability associated with its position

interactions.label: Group number
interactions.teaches: Moving column by column shows where group position reliably predicts ionic charge, where the rule changes from cations to anions, and where transition-metal groups are less predictable

interactions.label: Color scheme
interactions.teaches: Comparing type-based coloring with charge-based coloring separates chemical family membership from the actual ion charge an element commonly forms

demo_steps.title: Group 1: one electron lost
demo_steps.narration: Group 1 metals are highlighted as +1 cation formers. Their valence configurations end in one outer s electron, so losing that electron gives a stable noble-gas-like configuration.

demo_steps.title: Group 2: two electrons lost
demo_steps.narration: Group 2 metals form +2 ions for the same reason, but now two outer s electrons are removed. The group number directly predicts the charge for these main-group metals.

demo_steps.title: Transition-metal warning zone
demo_steps.narration: In the d-block, the highlighted column no longer gives a simple charge rule. Cells such as Cr, Fe, Cu, Au, and Hg show multiple common charges, so their ion charges must often be learned or inferred from compounds.

demo_steps.title: Nonmetals count back from the noble gases
demo_steps.narration: On the right side, nonmetals form anions by gaining enough electrons to reach a noble-gas configuration. Group 17 elements are one column left of the noble gases, so they typically form −1 ions.

demo_steps.title: Noble gases: no common ion
demo_steps.narration: The noble gases already have stable valence shells, so their cells carry no ion-charge labels. Their column acts as the reference point for the negative charges of nearby nonmetals.

demo_steps.title: Compare families with charges
demo_steps.narration: Switching to charge-value coloring reveals that periodic families and ion charges are related but not identical. The main-group pattern is clear, while the transition metals stand out as variable-charge exceptions.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Main-group ionic charge is largely a shortcut to the nearest noble-gas electron configuration, but transition metals do not obey a single group-number charge rule.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean 2D SVG periodic table matching the long-form layout in the source image: purple Group 1 cations, green Group 2 cations, tan d-block metals, pink/red-tinted anion-forming nonmetals, pale blue halogens, and cyan noble gases in the element-type view. Keep the printed ion labels large and bold inside cells, with multiple charges stacked on separate lines where shown. The group-number slider should highlight the entire selected column with a translucent vertical overlay without hiding the charge labels. The click detail panel should appear beside or below the table and include examples such as Na: [Ne]3s1 → Na+ by losing one electron; Cl: [Ne]3s2 3p5 → Cl− by gaining one electron; Fe: variable Fe2+/Fe3+ because transition-metal d electrons produce multiple stable cations. In charge-value mode, recolor cells by common charge categories such as +1, +2, +3, variable positive, −3, −2, −1, and no common ion, while preserving all cell labels and outlines.

authoredContext:
Note the usefulness of the periodic table in predicting likely ion formation and charge ( ). Moving from the far left to the right on the periodic table, main-group elements tend to form cations with a charge equal to the group number. That is, group 1 elements form 1+ ions; group 2 elements form 2+ ions, and so on. Moving from the far right to the left on the periodic table, elements often form anions with a negative charge equal to the number of groups moved left from the noble gases. For example, group 17 elements (one group left of the noble gases) form 1− ions; group 16 elements (two groups left) form 2− ions, and so on. This trend can be used as a guide in many cases, but its predictive value decreases when moving toward the center of the periodic table. In fact, transition metals and some other metals often exhibit variable charges that are not predictable by their location in the table. For example, copper can form ions with a 1+ or 2+ charge, and iron can form ions with a 2+ or 3+ charge.

Some elements exhibit a regular pattern of ionic charge when they form ions.

A periodic table showing common ion charges. Group one contains lithium superscript plus, sodium superscript plus, potassium superscript plus, rubidium superscript plus, cesium superscript plus, and francium superscript plus. Group two contains beryllium superscript 2 plus, magnesium superscript 2 plus, calcium superscript 2 plus, strontium superscript 2 plus, barium superscript 2 plus, and radium superscript 2 plus. Group six contains chromium superscript 3 plus and chromium superscript 6 plus. Group seven contains manganese superscript 2 plus. Group eight contains iron superscript 2 plus and iron superscript 3 plus. Group nine contains cobalt superscript 2 plus. Group ten contains nickel superscript 2 plus and platinum superscript 2 plus. Group 11 contains copper superscript plus and copper superscript 2 plus, silver superscript plus, and gold superscript plus and gold superscript 3 plus. Group 12 contains zinc superscript 2 plus, cadmium superscript 2 plus, and mercury superscript 2 plus and mercury subscript 2 superscript 2 plus. Group 13 contains aluminum superscript 3 plus. Group 14 contains carbon superscript 4 minus. Group 15 contains nitrogen superscript 3 minus, phosphorus superscript 3 minus, and arsenic superscript 3 minus. Group 16 contains oxygen superscript 2 minus, sulfur superscript 2 minus, selenium superscript 2 minus, and tellurium superscript 2 minus. Group 17 contains fluorine superscript minus, chlorine superscript minus, bromine superscript minus, iodine superscript minus, and astatine superscript minus. Group 18 contains helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, and radon, with no charges indicated.

The ions that we have discussed so far are called monatomic ions , that is, they are ions formed from only one atom. We also find many polyatomic ions . These ions, which act as discrete units, are electrically charged molecules (a group of bonded atoms with an overall charge). Some of the more important polyatomic ions are listed in . Oxyanions are polyatomic ions that contain one or more oxygen atoms. At this point in your study of chemistry, you should memorize the names, formulas, and charges of the most common polyatomic ions. Because you will use them repeatedly, they will soon become familiar.

discrepancies: The default state adds yellow/gold group-1 highlight outlines that are not present in the source static table, changing the clean reference appearance.
A large explanatory UI/control panel is visible at the right, so the periodic table occupies only part of the available width instead of appearing as the full-width standalone figure in the source.
The vertical purple 'Period' label is clipped/mispositioned at the far left and is barely readable compared with the source.
Because the table is compressed beside the UI, the title, group numbers, period numbers, and element/ion labels are noticeably smaller and less legible than in the source.
The red f-block pointer/arrow is only approximate and appears as multiple overlapping curves rather than the cleaner single curved red arrow in the source.
evaluation.notes: The periodic-table cell layout, ion labels, and family colors are very close to the source, but the default guided overlay, large side UI, clipped Period label, and reduced label legibility prevent it from being a clean drop-in replacement.
action_items: Make the default visual match the static source: remove or disable the yellow group highlight until the user interacts with the slider or demo controls.
Move the UI below the figure or make it collapsible so the periodic table fills the available inline width like the source image.
Reposition the rotated 'Period' label so it is fully visible and aligned with the period numbers.
Increase effective label readability at inline size, especially the title, group numbers, period numbers, and ion labels when the UI is present.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interactivity are strong, but the issues are implementation-level visual/layout problems such as default highlights, side UI placement, clipped labels, and arrow styling that the generator can fix.
